Connor Riley Moucka pleaded guilty in Seattle federal court on Wednesday to computer fraud, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and a related conspiracy over the 2024 breaches of Snowflake customer accounts. The intrusions reached at least 165 organizations and exposed records belonging to at least 100 million people. Moucka, 26, of Kitchener, Ontario, personally took at least $495,000 from

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] UNC5537 Snowflake cloud sign-in from known exfil IPs 45.27.26.205 / 37.19.210.21 · [LLM] Password-only single-factor success to cloud app with long-stale credential · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Endpoint / proxy egress to UNC5537 Snowflake exfil IPs 45.27.26.205 / 37.19.210.21 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
UNC5537 Snowflake cloud sign-in from known exfil IPs 45.27.26.205 / 37.19.210.21 AIExploitation Medium
Alerts on any successful Entra ID / federated-SaaS authentication originating from the two IP addresses Mandiant attributed to UNC5537's Snowflake data-theft campaign. These IPs were used to drive Python-Connector and DBeaver/JDBC sessions against victim Snowflake instances, so a success from them against any corporate identity is a direct hit on the actor's access infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the two hard IOC IPs from the article, independently confirmed by Mandiant (Python Connector on 45.27.26.205, DBeaver/JDBC on 37.19.210.21) — a success from either against any tenant identity is unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion • https://www.securityweek.com/snowflake-attacks-mandiant-links-data-breaches-to-infostealer-infections/
ATT&CKT1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel enrichment/sandbox VPN egressing from a recycled Mullvad/PIA exit node that now maps to one of these IPs
  • Penetration-test or red-team using a commercial VPN whose exit node reuses the IP
  • Security researcher reproducing the campaign from the same hosting range
  • IP reassigned by the hosting provider (ALEXHOST/VPN) to a benign tenant months later
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName has_any ("Snowflake", "PowerBI", "DBeaver", "Python") or ClientAppUsed !in~ ("Browser")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the AccountUpn, AppDisplayName (esp. Snowflake/data-warehouse or PowerBI connectors), ClientAppUsed and whether MFA was satisfied; pull all other sign-ins for that user in the last 90d. 2) Contain: disable the account, revoke refresh tokens/sessions, force password reset, and enforce MFA; block both IPs at the identity CA policy and perimeter. 3) Hunt: search all cloud data-store query/export logs for that session, and sweep every other identity that authenticated from these IPs or from the same VPN ASN.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in ("45.27.26.205", "37.19.210.21")
| where ErrorCode == 0                       // successful auth only
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName,
          IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, AuthenticationRequirement
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in ("45.27.26.205", "37.19.210.21")
| where ResultType == 0                      // successful auth only
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName,
          IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Password-only single-factor success to cloud app with long-stale credential AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exact weakness UNC5537 exploited: a successful single-factor (password-only) sign-in to a SaaS/cloud app by an account whose password has not been rotated in over a year. Mandiant found credentials harvested as far back as Nov 2020 still valid at intrusion time and 79.7% of used accounts had prior exposure — this surfaces the unrotated, MFA-less accounts before they are abused. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's root cause — password-only auth (MFA off) plus stale-never-rotated credentials — using AuthenticationRequirement=singleFactorAuthentication and LastPasswordChangeTimestamp>365d; Datadog/Sentinel lack the password-age field so those bodies fall back to single-factor only. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate service/human accounts on legacy apps that genuinely don't support MFA and rarely rotate passwords
  • Break-glass or emergency-access accounts intentionally single-factor
  • Kiosk / shared accounts with long-lived static passwords
  • Users on federated apps where MFA is asserted upstream and Entra logs it as single-factor
  • Automation accounts with old passwords by policy exception
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("LegacyLOB", "OnPremSSO") and AccountUpn !startswith "breakglass" and AccountUpn !startswith "svc-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by DaysSincePwdChange and by app sensitivity (data warehouse, HR/payroll, admin portals); flag any also seen from hosting/VPN ASNs. 2) Contain: for the highest-risk accounts, force password rotation and enroll MFA / apply a Conditional Access policy blocking single-factor for that app. 3) Hunt: pivot each stale account against leaked-credential feeds (infostealer logs) and review its recent data-access/export activity for bulk pulls.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0                                   // successful auth
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "singleFactorAuthentication"
| where IsInteractive == true
| where isnotempty(LastPasswordChangeTimestamp)
| where LastPasswordChangeTimestamp < ago(365d)          // 365d = unrotated; article cites creds valid up to 4 yrs
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| extend DaysSincePwdChange = datetime_diff('day', Timestamp, LastPasswordChangeTimestamp)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName,
          IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, LastPasswordChangeTimestamp, DaysSincePwdChange
| order by DaysSincePwdChange desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0                                  // successful auth
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "singleFactorAuthentication"
| where UserType =~ "Member"
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName,
          IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint / proxy egress to UNC5537 Snowflake exfil IPs 45.27.26.205 / 37.19.210.21 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags any host, proxy, or firewall connection to the two UNC5537-attributed IP addresses, catching the data-exfiltration / tooling channel (Python Connector and DBeaver/JDBC sessions) if the actor's infrastructure is reached from inside the estate. Complements the identity-side detections with a network pivot. Rationale: Reuses the two confirmed IOC IPs on the network plane; any internal host reaching them (esp. from python.exe/dbeaver.exe per Mandiant's client-app attribution) indicates actor tooling or exfil egress. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/threat-actor-breaches-snowflake/
ATT&CKT1567 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/OSINT scanner or IOC-validation tool deliberately probing the IPs
  • Commercial VPN client on an endpoint egressing to a reused Mullvad/PIA/ALEXHOST exit that now maps to the IP
  • Security researcher reproduction traffic
  • Provider reassignment of the IP to a benign service post-2024
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mullvad.exe", "pia.exe", "openvpn.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName (flag python.exe, dbeaver.exe, java.exe, JDBC clients) and the volume of bytes sent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block both IPs at the egress firewall/proxy, and capture the process for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate the source host/user with cloud-warehouse export activity and check whether the same identity appears in the identity-side detections (UC1/UC2) for a full initial-access→exfil chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.27.26.205", "37.19.210.21")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.27.26.205", "37.19.210.21")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName,
          DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.

                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | rename Processes.user as user]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNC5537 Snowflake data-theft: sign-in from attacker infrastructure IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts authentication events (including federated cloud/SaaS SSO such as Snowflake) originating from the two IP addresses attributed to the UNC5537 Snowflake extortion campaign (Moucka/Binns). Because impacted Snowflake tenants lacked MFA, any successful auth from these IPs indicates account takeover with infostealer-harvested credentials. Rationale: Pivots on the two campaign-attributed IPs (45.27.26.205 confirmed present in Snowflake access logs by Mandiant/Google Cloud; both listed as UNC5537 infrastructure). Any auth from these IPs against a no-MFA tenant is the exact TTP described. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion • https://therecord.media/guilty-plea-snowflake-hack-connor-riley-moucka • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/data-breach/snowflake-data-breach
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote employee egressing from a Mullvad/PIA VPN exit node that shares one of these IPs (UNC5537 used commercial VPNs — IP reuse is real)
  • IP reassigned by the VPS/VPN provider to a benign tenant months after the 2024 campaign
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel platform deliberately detonating/validating the IOC from a sandbox
  • Third-party pentest or red-team sourcing traffic through the same commercial VPN provider
Suppression filter
| where ResultType == 0 and (AppDisplayName has_any ("Snowflake","data") or isnotempty(AppDisplayName))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the account, target app (esp. Snowflake/data-warehouse SSO), and ResultType==0 (success). Check whether MFA was satisfied and whether the user has any prior sign-in from that ASN/geo. 2) CONTAIN: If success + no MFA, disable the account, revoke sessions/tokens, force password reset, and enforce MFA on the tenant. Block the IPs at IdP conditional access and perimeter. 3) HUNT: Pull all activity for that identity (bulk queries/exports, new API keys), search other identities authenticating from the same IPs/ASN, and check endpoints for infostealer infection (Vidar/LummaC2/RISEPRO) that may have leaked the credential.

union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs

| where IPAddress in ("45.27.26.205","37.19.210.21")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, ResultType, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNC5537 Snowflake campaign: network connection to attacker IPs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host/appliance/flow-log connection to or from the two IP addresses attributed to the UNC5537 Snowflake extortion campaign. Complements the identity-side detection by catching the same IOCs on endpoint EDR, firewall CEF, and cloud VPC-flow telemetry where SSO logs are unavailable. Rationale: Same two attributed campaign IPs, pivoted on network telemetry (endpoint EDR, firewall CEF, VPC flow) instead of identity — catches egress/exfil to attacker infra where SSO logs aren't collected. Large SentBytes/totalBytes to these IPs corroborates the terabyte-scale data theft described. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/data-breach/snowflake-data-breach

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • VPS IP reassigned to a benign service after the 2024 campaign window
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance or scanner beaconing the IOC for validation
  • Corporate proxy egress where the appliance IP coincidentally matches after provider reallocation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the internal host/appliance, the initiating process, direction, and byte volume. Outbound with large SentBytes = probable exfil; small/inbound may be scanning or reuse. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host if an interactive process initiated the connection; block both IPs egress at firewall/proxy; snapshot for forensics. 3) HUNT: Correlate with the identity-side detection (same IPs in SigninLogs), check the host for infostealer artifacts and stored Snowflake/DB credentials, and review data-warehouse query/export logs for bulk pulls in the same window.

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Nuxt dev server bound to non-loopback interface (nuxi/nuxt dev --host) · [LLM] Inbound non-loopback connection to Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe HMR port)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe) spawns shell or LOLBin child — DevTools RPC RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe) spawns shell or LOLBin child — DevTools RPC RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the payload-execution step of CVE-2026-71319, where the unauthenticated openInEditor()/updateOptions() RPC chain makes the launch-editor package spawn an attacker-controlled command as a child of the node.exe dev server. Scopes to node.exe whose command line indicates a Nuxt/Vite dev process spawning an interpreter or LOLBin — a combination that should never occur during normal 'nuxi dev'. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete chain (openInEditor -> launch-editor spawns child of the node.exe dev server) plus the specific process ancestry (node.exe parent whose cmdline contains nuxt/nuxi/vite/devtools -> interpreter/LOLBin child). Cross-checked GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv and the Nuxt v4.5 security blog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv • https://nuxt.com/blog/v4-5-security • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nuxt/devtools/CVE-2026-71319/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately configured 'openInEditor' to a shell wrapper that launches their editor (e.g. a cmd/powershell shim launching VS Code)
  • Nuxt/Vite build scripts invoking curl.exe to fetch assets during dev
  • A dev-tooling task runner spawning powershell for a lifecycle hook (postinstall-style scripts run via node)
  • node-based test runners shelling out to cmd.exe for OS-level test fixtures
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "code.exe" and ProcessCommandLine !has "code-insiders" and ProcessCommandLine !has "sublime_text" and ProcessCommandLine !has "webstorm" and ProcessCommandLine !has "idea64.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine. A benign hit shows an editor path (code.exe, sublime); a malicious hit shows arbitrary commands (whoami, curl to external IP, base64, reverse-shell one-liners). Confirm the node.exe process is a nuxi/vite dev server. 2) Contain: kill the node dev-server process tree, isolate the developer workstation, and force-update @nuxt/devtools to >=3.3.1 (lockfile refresh). 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound non-loopback connections to the node.exe listening port just before the spawn, and review the child process's own children/network egress for follow-on payloads or credential access.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxt","nuxi","vite",".nuxt","devtools")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxt","nuxi","vite",".nuxt","devtools")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","curl.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nuxt dev server bound to non-loopback interface (nuxi/nuxt dev --host) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the risky exposure configuration the CVE-2026-71319 advisory explicitly warns against: running the dev server with '--host', which binds the Vite HMR / DevTools RPC socket to a non-loopback interface and makes the unauthenticated RPC channel reachable by any LAN peer. This is a posture/initial-access hunt for exposed dev servers before exploitation. Rationale: Directly encodes the advisory's named risky invocation 'nuxi dev --host' as the exposure signal — it is the one config that turns a same-host-only bug into a LAN-reachable RCE. High-signal because '--host' on a dev command is deliberate and uncommon. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv • https://nuxt.com/blog/v4-5-security
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer intentionally using --host to test on a mobile device over the same Wi-Fi
  • CI/preview pipelines that bind dev servers with --host inside an isolated container network
  • Team using --host on a trusted, firewalled dev VLAN by policy
  • Docker-based dev where --host is required for port forwarding to reach the container
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is on an untrusted/shared network and whether @nuxt/devtools is < 3.3.1 on that project. Note the listening port from the command line. 2) Contain: advise the developer to drop --host (or restrict to loopback), or patch @nuxt/devtools to >=3.3.1 / set devtools:{enabled:false}. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (node.exe spawning interpreters) and to inbound connections on the dev-server port from non-loopback sources on this host during the exposure window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxi","nuxt")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dev"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--host"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxi","nuxt")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dev"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--host"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound non-loopback connection to Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe HMR port) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a remote peer connecting to the Vite HMR / DevTools RPC listener hosted by node.exe from a non-loopback address — the network precondition for CVE-2026-71319 exploitation over the LAN. Because the vulnerable RPC channel is normally only reached via localhost, any inbound accept from a non-loopback source to a nuxt/vite node process is anomalous and worth pairing with UC1. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's stated LAN reach ('any peer on the LAN when the dev server is bound with nuxi dev --host'). Scopes inbound accepts to node.exe dev processes and excludes loopback, isolating the exact network shape an off-host attacker must produce. Sentinel left blank: no available tenant table reliably attributes inbound socket accepts to the node.exe process. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nuxt/devtools/CVE-2026-71319/
ATT&CKT1190 T1021
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • Another workstation on the dev subnet legitimately previewing a colleague's dev build
  • Container/host networking where the bridge presents a non-loopback source IP for local traffic
  • Local network scanners / asset-inventory tools probing the open dev port
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteIP — is it a known developer device or an unexpected/unknown LAN host? Check what LocalPort node.exe was listening on and whether --host was used (UC2). 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, isolate the workstation, kill the node dev server, and patch @nuxt/devtools to >=3.3.1. 3) Hunt: correlate the inbound connection timestamp with UC1 (node.exe spawning an interpreter/LOLBin) on the same host within a short window — a spawn shortly after the inbound accept is strong evidence of successful RPC exploitation.

BleepingComputer
2026-08-05 6 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers exploited a SQL injection vulnerability to install a post-exploitation toolkit directly inside an Oracle database that was used to breach a corporate network. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Oracle DB process (oracle.exe) spawning cmd.exe/PowerShell - khunt KhuntCmd OS command exec
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM registry hive dump descending from Oracle DB process (khunt cred theft) · [LLM] khunt service enumeration - tasklist /svc output written to khunttasks.txt · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Oracle DB process (oracle.exe) spawning cmd.exe/PowerShell - khunt KhuntCmd OS command exec AIInstallation High
Hunts the core khunt technique: the Oracle embedded-JVM host process (oracle.exe / extproc.exe) directly spawning a Windows command interpreter to run OS commands (e.g. 'cmd.exe /c whoami'). An Oracle database server process should never be the parent of cmd.exe or powershell.exe - this is the SQL-injection-to-RCE bridge Huntress documented. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact chain: Oracle JVM host process executing 'cmd.exe /c whoami' with SYSTEM rights. FalconForce independently documents oracle.exe->cmd.exe as the code-execution signature and names conhost.exe/oradmin.exe as the benign children to filter, so the FP surface is tiny. Cross-checked against: • https://medium.com/falconforce/falcon-friday-detecting-code-execution-through-microsoft-sql-server-and-oracle-database-b8fbef83fa4e • https://attack.mitre.org/datacomponents/DC0064/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1505.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA using Oracle DBMS_SCHEDULER external jobs to run legitimate maintenance batch scripts
  • Oracle installer/patch (opatch) invoking cmd.exe during upgrades
  • Monitoring agents that shell out from an Oracle wrapper service
  • Custom in-house PL/SQL that legitimately calls host commands via a Java stored proc
  • Oracle backup jobs (RMAN) spawning shell helpers
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd has_any ("whoami","tasklist","reg save","hklm","net user","net localgroup","powershell") or ParentCmd has_any ("Khunt","CREATE JAVA")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull ChildCmd - confirm reconnaissance/creds intent ('whoami','tasklist','reg save'); check whether this oracle.exe has ever spawned cmd.exe before (30d baseline). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the DB host, capture the Oracle listener + Apache access logs, and query the DB for attacker Java objects (SELECT owner,name FROM all_java_classes WHERE name LIKE 'Khunt%'; DROP them) and revoke the app account's JAVASYSPRIV/permissions. 3) HUNT: Pivot to same host for SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive copies and khunttasks.txt, and review Tomcat access logs for the autocomplete-search SQLi and source IP 178.162.151.229.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("oracle.exe","extproc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","oradmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\oracle.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\extproc.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\whoami.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM registry hive dump descending from Oracle DB process (khunt cred theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access step where the khunt-controlled Oracle process chain copies the SAM, SECURITY and SYSTEM registry hives (via reg save / esentutl / copy) to recover local Windows password hashes. Requires Oracle ancestry so it fires only on the article's DB-server-initiated hive theft, not routine admin backups. Rationale: Ties the generic hive-dump verbs (reg save / esentutl / copy of SAM+SECURITY+SYSTEM) to Oracle process ancestry, matching Huntress's statement that the khunt operators copied all three hives from the DB host for offline hash recovery. The Oracle-ancestry gate removes the routine-backup FP that plagues bare hive-dump rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-run-khunt-post-exploitation-toolkit-from-oracle-database/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/002/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DFIR/forensics acquisition run from the DB host
  • Sysadmin taking a SAM backup before a password-policy change
  • Backup software (Veeam/NetBackup agent) invoking esentutl for VSS-consistent copies
  • Oracle patch tooling touching SYSTEM hive paths
  • Vulnerability scanner credentialed check dumping registry
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","bengine.exe") or ChildCmd has_any ("veeam","netbackup","forensic"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the full ancestry back to oracle.exe and identify the output hive files' path; if grandparent is oracle.exe treat as confirmed breach. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, force-rotate ALL local account passwords and the KRBTGT if the box is domain-joined, and preserve the copied .hiv files as evidence. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceFileEvents for the resulting SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM copies and any archive (KhuntUnzip) or outbound transfer; scope other Oracle/Tomcat hosts for the same oracle.exe->reg.exe pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "oracle.exe" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "oracle.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("reg.exe","esentutl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","xcopy.exe","robocopy.exe")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"hklm\sam", @"hklm\security", @"hklm\system"))
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "sam" and ProcessCommandLine has "security" and ProcessCommandLine has "system")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "esentutl" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\config\sam", @"\config\security", @"\config\system"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\oracle.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"

     or (CommandLine has "esentutl" and (CommandLine has "config\\sam" or CommandLine has "config\\security" or CommandLine has "config\\system"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

khunt service enumeration - tasklist /svc output written to khunttasks.txt AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the khunt discovery artifact: 'tasklist /svc' redirected into the hard-coded filename khunttasks.txt. The output filename is unique to this toolkit, making the string a near-zero-FP indicator; also fires on the tasklist /svc command when it descends from the Oracle DB process. Rationale: khunttasks.txt is a hard-coded, toolkit-specific output filename with essentially no legitimate use, so it is a golden string; the secondary tasklist /svc + oracle.exe parent clause catches the discovery even if the operator renames the output file. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-run-khunt-post-exploitation-toolkit-from-oracle-database/
ATT&CKT1007 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin diagnostic script that happens to redirect tasklist /svc to a text file (won't match the khunttasks.txt string, only the tasklist+oracle clause)
  • Monitoring tool inventorying services on the DB host
  • IR responder running tasklist /svc during triage on the same box
  • Batch job named similarly by coincidence (extremely unlikely to contain literal khunttasks.txt)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: If khunttasks.txt is present, treat as confirmed khunt activity - retrieve the file and its parent process ancestry. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Oracle host, snapshot for forensics, and drop the malicious Java DB objects (Khunt* classes) plus revoke the app account's Java/OS-exec privileges. 3) HUNT: Correlate with the oracle.exe->cmd.exe execution and the SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive-dump detections on the same host and timeframe; check for KhuntUnzip archive creation and outbound exfil.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ProcessCommandLine has "khunttasks.txt"
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "tasklist" and ProcessCommandLine has "/svc"
         and (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "oracle.exe" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "oracle.exe"))
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FileName =~ "khunttasks.txt"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="File", Detail=FolderPath, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "khunttasks.txt"
     or (CommandLine has "tasklist" and CommandLine has "/svc" and ParentProcessName endswith "\\oracle.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Over 250 ClickFix Domains Use Browser Fingerprinting to Hide macOS Malware Lures

The Hacker NewsMicrosoft Security Blog
2026-08-05 15 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A macOS ClickFix campaign shifted tactics from openly serving infostealer lures to hiding them behind a browser-fingerprinting gate. The change makes malicious infrastructure harder to detect while giving defenders new hunting opportunities. The post From open lures to cloaked gates: How a macOS ClickFix campaign learned to hide appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1027 T1176 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1486 T1555.003
Domainsapricotfilepoint.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] macOS ClickFix delivery-domain contact (apricotfilepoint + 'file'-token DGA cluster) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] macOS ClickFix Terminal curl|base64|gunzip staging execution · [LLM] macOS Gatekeeper/quarantine bypass (xattr -c) + chmod +x on downloaded ClickFix payload · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
macOS ClickFix delivery-domain contact (apricotfilepoint + 'file'-token DGA cluster) AIDelivery High
Hunts macOS endpoints and network appliances contacting the Microsoft-confirmed cluster of algorithmically-named 'file'-token ClickFix domains (e.g. apricotfilepoint[.]com, filecopperbasket[.]sbs) or the shared /curl/<id> staging path that fronts AMOS/MacSync delivery. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact confirmed domain list and the /curl/ staging artifact rather than a generic newly-registered-domain heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact 17-domain cluster and the /curl/<id> staging path Microsoft published; both were cross-checked against the Microsoft Security Blog and the gbhackers write-up, so these are second-sourced IOCs rather than article-only claims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/05/macos-clickfix-campaign-learned-hide/ • https://gbhackers.com/250-fake-download-domains/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox intentionally browsing the domains for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance auto-resolving IOC domains
  • A legitimate internal path containing the substring '/curl/' being matched by the secondary RemoteUrl clause
  • Passive-DNS or DNS-sinkhole telemetry replaying the domain to a honeypot
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("com.apple.Safari.SafeBrowsing.Service") and RemoteUrl has_any (clickfix_domains)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the querying host is macOS and identify the initiating browser process and user; check whether the request reached a /curl/ path (staging) vs. only the front-end domain. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domain cluster at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a /curl/ fetch or subsequent shell execution is seen. 3) Hunt: pivot on that host for the Terminal curl|base64|gunzip execution chain (UC 2) and xattr/chmod quarantine bypass (UC 3), and sweep the org for any other host resolving the same cluster.
let clickfix_domains = dynamic(["applefilevault.com","apricotfilepoint.com","bananafastfile.com","cloudfilebridge.com","filecedarwallet.online","filecopperbasket.sbs","filecrimsonsignal.online","filemarblegarden.sbs","fileoceanhammer.sbs","filerubyfolder.sbs","filevelvettractor.sbs","lemonfilewave.com","limefilescope.com","mangocloudfile.com","orangesmartfile.com","syncdatavault.com","cloudsendhub.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (clickfix_domains) or RemoteUrl has "/curl/"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let clickfix_domains = dynamic(["applefilevault.com","apricotfilepoint.com","bananafastfile.com","cloudfilebridge.com","filecedarwallet.online","filecopperbasket.sbs","filecrimsonsignal.online","filemarblegarden.sbs","fileoceanhammer.sbs","filerubyfolder.sbs","filevelvettractor.sbs","lemonfilewave.com","limefilescope.com","mangocloudfile.com","orangesmartfile.com","syncdatavault.com","cloudsendhub.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (clickfix_domains)
   | project TimeGenerated, Src = SrcIpAddr, Host = SrcHostname, Indicator = DnsQuery, Kind = "dns"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DestinationHostName has_any (clickfix_domains) or RequestURL has_any (clickfix_domains) or RequestURL has "/curl/"
   | project TimeGenerated, Src = SourceIP, Host = DestinationHostName, Indicator = RequestURL, Kind = "proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS ClickFix Terminal curl|base64|gunzip staging execution AIInstallation High
Hunts the paste-to-Terminal execution stage of the macOS ClickFix chain: a shell (zsh/bash/sh) or curl invocation pulling from a /curl/ staging path and decoding the payload with base64/gunzip before running it via osascript/shell. Article-specific because it chains the exact utilities and staging path Microsoft documented rather than any curl usage. Rationale: Anchors on the exact utility chain (curl -> base64/gunzip -> zsh/osascript) and the /curl/<id> staging path Microsoft named; the combination is far more specific than generic curl-pipe-to-shell and was corroborated by the Microsoft blog. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/05/macos-clickfix-campaign-learned-hide/ • https://gbhackers.com/250-fake-download-domains/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a legitimate 'curl ... | bash' installer (e.g. Homebrew, rustup, nvm)
  • CI/build agents on macOS invoking curl piped to shell for tooling setup
  • IT admin bootstrap scripts that base64-decode config then execute
  • Package managers using gunzip on downloaded tarballs in the same command line
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("brew.sh","raw.githubusercontent.com","sh.rustup.rs","get.docker.com","nvm.sh"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine — confirm the fetch host resolves to the ClickFix cluster and the /curl/ path, and identify the parent (Terminal.app is expected for ClickFix). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the shell chain, and block the staging host; snapshot ~/Downloads, /tmp and /var/folders for the dropped Mach-O. 3) Hunt: look for AMOS/MacSync behaviour on that host — keychain dumping, browser-profile and crypto-wallet access, SSH-key reads, and archive staging/exfil to the same infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/curl/"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64","gunzip") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("| bash","| sh","| zsh","bash -c","sh -c","zsh -c","osascript"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/curl/"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64","gunzip") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("| bash","| sh","| zsh","bash -c","sh -c","zsh -c","osascript"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS Gatekeeper/quarantine bypass (xattr -c) + chmod +x on downloaded ClickFix payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-download defense-evasion step of the macOS ClickFix chain: stripping the com.apple.quarantine attribute with xattr and marking a downloaded file executable with chmod +x in ~/Downloads, /tmp or /var/folders before running AMOS/MacSync. Article-specific because Microsoft's detection guidance calls out the exact 'xattr -c' and 'chmod +x' sequence used by this campaign. Rationale: Uses the specific 'xattr -c' / com.apple.quarantine and 'chmod +x' in Downloads/tmp sequence that Microsoft's write-up flags for this campaign, scoped to user-download paths to keep it AMOS/MacSync-specific rather than any chmod. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/05/macos-clickfix-campaign-learned-hide/
ATT&CKT1553.001 T1222.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running chmod +x on a legitimately downloaded script or binary in ~/Downloads
  • Homebrew/pip/npm post-install steps that chmod downloaded tooling
  • Security tooling or admin manually clearing quarantine on a trusted app with xattr -c
  • Build pipelines unpacking and marking artifacts executable under /var/folders
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("zsh","bash","sh","Terminal","curl") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("zsh","bash","sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the target file path and whether it was fetched by the ClickFix curl chain (UC 2) or resolved to the domain cluster (UC 1); check the file's signature/notarization status. 2) Contain: quarantine or delete the target Mach-O, isolate the host, and capture the file hash for org-wide sweeping. 3) Hunt: on confirmation, look for stealer behaviour — keychain/login-keychain access, browser Login Data / cookies reads, ~/.ssh key access, crypto-wallet directory reads, and zip/tar staging followed by egress to the staging infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "xattr" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c","com.apple.quarantine"))
     or (FileName =~ "chmod" and ProcessCommandLine has "+x" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Downloads/","/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/var/folders/"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "xattr" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c","com.apple.quarantine"))
     or (FileName =~ "chmod" and ProcessCommandLine has "+x" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Downloads/","/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/var/folders/"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
