Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

COLDCARD security-audit phishing lure from coldcardteamnews.com / coldcardcompliance.com AIDelivery High
Hunts the Proofpoint-reported phishing wave impersonating COLDCARD's 'Hardware audit now available' notice. Pivots on the specific sender domain, subject and the coldcardcompliance.com lure URL rather than a generic phishing template. Rationale: Uses the exact sender domain (compliance@coldcardteamnews.com), the verbatim subject 'Hardware audit now available', and the coldcardcompliance.com lure domain named by Proofpoint/BleepingComputer — all campaign-unique, so FP risk is minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coldcard-security-audit-phishing-attack-installs-remote-access-tool/
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security-awareness team forwarding the phishing sample for analysis
  • A user replying to/quoting the lure so the subject/domain appears intra-org
  • Threat-intel mailbox that intentionally ingests malicious samples
  • COLDCARD legitimate comms if they ever adopt a similarly worded audit subject (verify sender domain is the real coldcard.com)
Suppression filter
| where not (RecipientEmailAddress has_any ("soc@","phishing@","abuse@","security@"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SenderFromDomain is coldcardteamnews.com (not the legitimate coldcard.com) and DeliveryAction=Delivered; pull the recipient list and any UrlClickEvents for coldcardcompliance.com. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block coldcardteamnews.com + coldcardcompliance.com at the mail gateway and proxy. 3) Hunt: for every recipient who clicked, check the endpoint for Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat download and certutil-decoded setup.msi/docusign.exe (see companion UCs).
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let LureDomains = dynamic(["coldcardteamnews.com","coldcardcompliance.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (LureDomains)
   or SenderMailFromDomain in~ (LureDomains)
   or (Subject has "Hardware audit" and Subject has_any ("COLDCARD","Coldcard","audit now available"))
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
          Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

  ) on NetworkMessageId

certutil decodes embedded setup.msi / docusign.exe from Coldcard batch dropper AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage behaviour where the 25.7MB Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat writes two Base64 blobs to a random temp directory and decodes them to setup.msi (ScreenConnect) and docusign.exe (DocuSign decoy) using certutil. Rationale: certutil 'decode' plus the campaign-specific output filenames setup.msi and docusign.exe (both named and VirusTotal-linked in the article) is a very high-fidelity pairing — certutil is rarely used to decode an MSI+EXE into a temp dir in benign activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coldcard-security-audit-phishing-attack-installs-remote-access-tool/
ATT&CKT1140 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/IT using certutil -decode for legitimate cert/base64 workflows (rarely targeting .msi/.exe)
  • Software packaging pipelines that base64-transport an installer
  • Security researchers detonating this exact sample in a lab
  • EDR/AV self-test tooling that exercises certutil decoding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","explorer.exe") and (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Coldcard" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Temp\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is a .bat/cmd.exe (Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat) and the output landed in a random %TEMP% subfolder; grab SHA256 of setup.msi/docusign.exe and check VirusTotal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the certutil/msiexec/docusign.exe chain, and preserve %TEMP% before the script self-deletes it. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for activeretirementrelocation.com (ScreenConnect C2) and search the org for the parent Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat by name/hash.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "certutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "decode"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.msi","docusign.exe")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\Temp\" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (".msi",".exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "decode"
| where CommandLine has_any ("setup.msi","docusign.exe")
   or (CommandLine has "\\Temp\\" and CommandLine has_any (".msi",".exe"))
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Certutil Decodes Coldcard Phishing Payloads to Temp
id: 7b6e2c14-9d3a-4f21-8c7e-2a1f0b6d4e55
description: Detects certutil.exe decoding Base64 blobs to setup.msi/docusign.exe from the Coldcard security-audit phishing batch dropper.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coldcard-security-audit-phishing-attack-installs-remote-access-tool/

logsource:

detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\certutil.exe'
  selection_decode:

  selection_payload:

      - 'setup.msi'
      - 'docusign.exe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_decode and selection_payload
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\CERTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*decode* AND (*setup.msi* OR *docusign.exe*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/certutil\.exe$/i
| regex("decode", field=CommandLine)
| CommandLine=/(setup\.msi|docusign\.exe)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=certutil.exe AND (Processes.process="*-decode*" OR Processes.process="*/decode*" OR Processes.process="*decode*") AND (Processes.process="*setup.msi*" OR Processes.process="*docusign.exe*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat self-elevates via PowerShell UAC relaunch AIExploitation Medium
Detects the batch dropper's privilege-escalation step: when not already admin it uses PowerShell Start-Process -Verb RunAs to relaunch itself with a UAC prompt. Anchored on the campaign-specific batch filename and the RunAs relaunch pattern. Rationale: Ties the campaign-unique filename Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat to the PowerShell -Verb RunAs self-elevation the article describes (black window + UAC 'click Yes'), making it far more specific than a generic UAC-bypass rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coldcard-security-audit-phishing-attack-installs-remote-access-tool/
ATT&CKT1548.002 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit installers that self-elevate via PowerShell RunAs (but not named Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool)
  • IT scripts that relaunch elevated for maintenance
  • Sandbox detonation of this sample
  • Renamed copies of the batch — name filter would miss those, so treat absence as non-conclusive
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the batch filename and that the elevated relaunch was user-approved via UAC; capture the %TEMP% working dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the elevated PowerShell/batch chain, and revoke the local session. 3) Hunt: check for certutil-decoded setup.msi/docusign.exe on the same host and outbound connections to activeretirementrelocation.com; search email logs for the coldcardteamnews.com lure to the same user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "RunAs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool"
   or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "RunAs"
| where CommandLine has "Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool" or ParentProcessName has "Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ScreenConnect C2 beacon to activeretirementrelocation.com (COLDCARD campaign) AICommand & Control High
Detects the installed ConnectWise ScreenConnect client (delivered as setup.msi) beaconing to the threat actor's C2 domain activeretirementrelocation.com. Covers both the DNS lookup and the outbound connection for the campaign-specific C2. Rationale: activeretirementrelocation.com is the specific ScreenConnect C2 domain Proofpoint attributed to this threat actor; any resolution/connection to it is an unambiguous IOC hit regardless of the resolving process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/coldcard-security-audit-phishing-attack-installs-remote-access-tool/
ATT&CKT1219 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliance resolving the domain for analysis
  • Proxy/DNS security tooling pre-resolving IOC lists
  • An unrelated legitimate site later reusing the same domain after takedown (verify WHOIS/date)
  • Analyst manually browsing the domain during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox.exe","threatanalyzer.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection (expect a ScreenConnect client / setup.msi-installed service) and confirm ConnectWise ScreenConnect isn't an approved RMM in your environment. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block activeretirementrelocation.com at DNS/proxy/firewall, and uninstall the rogue ScreenConnect client + kill its service. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts resolving the domain, review ScreenConnect session logs for actor actions (data/crypto theft, further payloads), and check for ransomware-staging behaviour given Proofpoint's warning.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "activeretirementrelocation.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "activeretirementrelocation.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposed hosts carrying the three CISA KEV CVEs (Langflow / N-central / Tomcat) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow CVE-2026-9198 auth-bypass chain: /api/v1/auto_login then /api/v1/validate/code · [LLM] Langflow (python/uvicorn) server process spawning shell or download tool — CVE-2026-9198 RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Apache Tomcat (catalina/java) spawning shell — CVE-2026-34486 deserialization reverse shell
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tomcat java process making outbound connection to public IP — in-JVM reverse-shell callback
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow CVE-2026-9198 auth-bypass chain: /api/v1/auto_login then /api/v1/validate/code AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-9198 exploit chain where an unauthenticated caller first hits /api/v1/auto_login to mint a SUPERUSER token, then POSTs to /api/v1/validate/code to run attacker Python via exec(). Correlates both endpoints from one source IP inside a short window — the exact two-request sequence the public PoC uses. Rationale: Uses the two literal PoC endpoints for CVE-2026-9198 (/api/v1/auto_login, /api/v1/validate/code) confirmed by SentinelOne's vuln DB and The Hacker News; requiring both from one src in 10m makes this near-zero-FP versus a single-endpoint match. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-9198/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-flags-langflow-rce-tomcat-and-n.html • https://mallory.ai/stories/019faf4b-1bc7-791f-a8ef-a737b287d10d
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Langflow UI users legitimately validating flow code via /api/v1/validate/code (but paired with /auto_login from an external IP is not normal)
  • Automated Langflow health-check/synthetic monitors that call both endpoints
  • DAST/vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Nuclei) probing the KEV CVE
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy source-NAT collapsing many clients to one IP inflating the correlation
  • Langflow SSO/proxy setups where auto_login is the intended login path
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")  // drop loopback/health-check callers
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending SrcIpAddr in the 10m window; confirm /auto_login returned a token and /validate/code carried a Python body (look for import os/subprocess/exec). Check whether the IP is external/unexpected. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, isolate the Langflow host, and rotate/revoke any SUPERUSER API tokens; take the instance off the internet until patched to 1.10.1. 3) Hunt: pivot to host process telemetry (UC 'Langflow Python RCE') for python/uvicorn spawning shells, and check for new files, cron/systemd persistence, and outbound connections from the Langflow host.
let win = 10m;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/api/v1/auto_login", "/api/v1/validate/code")
| summarize AutoLogin = countif(Url has "/api/v1/auto_login"),
            ValidateCode = countif(Url has "/api/v1/validate/code"),
            Urls = make_set(Url, 20), Requests = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
| where AutoLogin > 0 and ValidateCode > 0   // both stages of the chain from one source in a 10m bucket
| order by LastSeen desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval autologin=if(like(url,"%/api/v1/auto_login%"),1,0), validatecode=if(like(url,"%/api/v1/validate/code%"),1,0)
| stats sum(autologin) as autologin_hits sum(validatecode) as validatecode_hits values(url) as urls by src _time
| where autologin_hits>0 AND validatecode_hits>0

Langflow (python/uvicorn) server process spawning shell or download tool — CVE-2026-9198 RCE AIExploitation High
Post-exploitation of CVE-2026-9198: the /validate/code exec() runs inside the Langflow Python process, so hands-on-keyboard activity surfaces as the langflow/uvicorn process spawning /bin/sh, bash, curl, wget or netcat. Scopes the parent to the Langflow backend via its command line so it isn't a generic 'python spawns bash' rule. Rationale: CVE-2026-9198's exec() runs in-process, so the high-fidelity signal is the Langflow/uvicorn parent (scoped by 'langflow'/'uvicorn' in the parent cmdline, per the fixed-in-1.10.1 OSS package) spawning a shell/download tool; the reverse-shell cmdline regex removes benign python subprocess noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-9198/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-flags-langflow-rce-tomcat-and-n.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow flows that legitimately shell out (custom components invoking curl/git/bash) as designed by the developer
  • pip/uv installs during Langflow component loading spawning sh -c
  • Container entrypoints where uvicorn is PID1 and spawns healthcheck shells
  • Data-science flows launching python3 subprocesses for model inference
  • Ops automation (Ansible) running commands under the Langflow service account
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/"," -e ","bash -i","nc ","ncat ","curl ","wget ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, nc -e, bash -i) or downloads; correlate the timestamp against web logs for a preceding /api/v1/validate/code POST (UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the langflow/uvicorn process tree, and snapshot for forensics; revoke Langflow SUPERUSER tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the shell child, new cron/systemd units, SSH authorized_keys changes, and outbound connections from the host to attacker infra.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow", "uvicorn")   // scope parent to Langflow backend
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "uvicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow", "uvicorn")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "uvicorn")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","curl","wget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Apache Tomcat (catalina/java) spawning shell — CVE-2026-34486 deserialization reverse shell AIInstallation High
Hunts the knaithe/KnYuan campaign's Java-deserialization reverse shells planted via CVE-2026-34486 (EncryptInterceptor bypass): the Tomcat java process, scoped by catalina/tomcat in its command line, spawning sh/bash/cmd/powershell/netcat. A web/app server spawning an interactive shell is a canonical exploitation tell. Rationale: Unit 42/SOCRadar confirm CVE-2026-34486 was used to plant Java-deserialization reverse shells; scoping the java parent by catalina/tomcat cmdline makes 'web server spawns shell' a high-fidelity, low-FP exploitation signal specific to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-34486-apache-tomcat-tribes-rce/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-deepseek-ai/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-flags-langflow-rce-tomcat-and-n.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tomcat apps that legitimately shell out (CI/CD agents, Jenkins on Tomcat invoking bash/git)
  • Startup/shutdown scripts where catalina.sh spawns sh for env setup
  • Monitoring agents executing shell healthchecks under the Tomcat JVM
  • Admin running scripts as the tomcat service account
  • Java apps invoking system utilities (ImageMagick, pdf tools) via Runtime.exec
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","whoami"," id","-enc","nc ","ncat ","bash -i","powershell -")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine for reverse-shell/recon (whoami, id, /dev/tcp, powershell -enc) and check the Tomcat access log for a preceding cluster/EncryptInterceptor exploit request. 2) Contain: isolate the server, kill the java→shell tree, and block outbound to any observed C2; disable the AJP/cluster listener if exposed. 3) Hunt: look for dropped webshells under webapps/, outbound connections from java (UC 'Tomcat java egress'), and lateral movement from the host; scope other internet-facing Tomcat instances for the same java→shell pattern.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

Tomcat java process making outbound connection to public IP — in-JVM reverse-shell callback AICommand & Control Medium
Catches CVE-2026-34486 reverse shells that open a socket inside the JVM (no child process) — invisible to the java-spawns-shell rule. Flags the Tomcat java process, scoped by catalina/tomcat cmdline, initiating an outbound connection to a public IP; a server-side web app should almost never dial out to the internet. Rationale: Reverse shells from Java deserialization frequently open the socket in-JVM without a child process, so a network-egress pivot on the Tomcat java process (public dest) complements the process-spawn UC and catches what it misses; keyed to the CVE-2026-34486 campaign behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-34486-apache-tomcat-tribes-rce/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-deepseek-ai/
ATT&CKT1571 T1219 T1059.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tomcat apps making legitimate outbound API/webhook calls (payment gateways, OAuth, S3)
  • Update/telemetry checks from the JVM or app dependencies
  • Log-forwarding or APM agents embedded in the JVM shipping to a SaaS endpoint
  • Maven/artifact fetches at app startup
  • Reverse-proxied microservice calls that egress via NAT to a public IP
Suppression filter
| where RemotePort !in (443, 80)  // known-good app egress is usually TLS/HTTP; reverse shells favour arbitrary ports
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich RemoteIP with threat intel and passive DNS; check whether the port is non-standard/long-lived and whether the app has any legitimate reason to reach that destination. 2) Contain: block the destination at the firewall/EDR, isolate the host if the IP is malicious, and capture the JVM for memory forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate with the java-spawns-shell UC and Tomcat access logs for the exploit request; sweep other Tomcat hosts for egress to the same IP/ASN.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","java.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","org.apache.catalina","tomcat")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Conns = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc

Exposed hosts carrying the three CISA KEV CVEs (Langflow / N-central / Tomcat) AIReconnaissance High
Attack-surface hunt: surfaces managed hosts whose vulnerability inventory shows any of the exact KEV CVEs from this CISA alert, prioritising internet-facing devices. Turns the KEV directive into an actionable patch/isolate worklist scoped to CVE-2026-9198, -0770, -18576, -34486, -29146. Rationale: Uses the five exact CVE identifiers CISA added to the KEV catalog in this alert; joining to DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing prioritises the exposed Langflow/N-central/Tomcat instances that the three-day mitigation deadline targets. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-flags-langflow-rce-tomcat-and-n.html • https://www.securityweek.com/cisa-warns-of-exploited-langflow-n-central-and-tomcat-vulnerabilities/amp/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices already patched but not yet rescanned by TVM (stale inventory shows the CVE)
  • Internal-only lab/test instances flagged as vulnerable but not reachable from the internet
  • Compensating controls (WAF/virtual patch) in place though the software version still matches
  • IsInternetFacing not populated for network-appliance-hosted N-central, under-reporting exposure
  • Third-party managed N-central instances outside the org's patch authority
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort by IsInternetFacing and severity; confirm the running version against the fixed builds (Langflow 1.10.1, N-central 2026.3, patched Tomcat) to drop already-remediated hosts. 2) Contain: expedite patching/emergency hotfix on exposed hosts; where patching lags, restrict inbound access or take the service offline per the CISA deadline. 3) Hunt: for each exposed host, run the exploitation UCs (Langflow API chain, Langflow/Tomcat process-spawn, java egress) over the pre-patch window to confirm none were already compromised.

Poison Claude Sells Discounted Claude Access While Its Operator Sees Every Customer Prompt

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered more than half-a-dozen services advertisements for illegal access to artificial intelligence (AI) models on underground cybercrime forums and messaging platforms. One such service, Poison Claude, claims to offer access to Anthropic's large language models (LLMs), including Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, and Sonnet 4.6. "Advertisements for Poison Claude

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Claude Code redirected to a rogue endpoint via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN env var
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Egress to Poison Claude / Ecomagent LLM relay proxy domains (prompt exfiltration)
Egress to Poison Claude / Ecomagent LLM relay proxy domains (prompt exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network connections to the Poison Claude and Ecomagent gray-market LLM relay domains. Because these services are gateway proxies, every prompt a developer sends through them (potentially containing source code, secrets, or customer data) is forwarded to and visible to the operator — so any resolution of these domains from a corporate host is an unsanctioned-AI data-egress event. Rationale: Anchored on the exact relay domains named by Okta (claudeopus.shop, api.claudeopus.shop, poison-claude.bitsender.top, ecomagent.in); base-domain contains-matching catches every subdomain. These are attacker-controlled proxies with no legitimate business use, so resolution = confirmed unsanctioned-AI egress. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/poison-claude-sells-discounted-claude.html • https://abvcreative.medium.com/the-90-discount-on-claude-tokens-has-a-small-catch-you-may-be-the-product-d0ee12154cbf
ATT&CKT1567 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel platform manually browsing/detonating the IOC domain during investigation
  • Automated URL sandbox or web-proxy link-preview prefetching the domain
  • Unrelated tenant on the shared bitsender.top parent domain (dynamic-host provider) — verify the full FQDN is poison-claude.bitsender.top
  • Security scanner / EDR reputation lookup resolving the domain for classification
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and user, and the InitiatingProcessFileName that made the connection — confirm it's a dev tool (node.exe/claude/curl) rather than a browser tab or sandbox. Pull the process command line for the API key. 2) Contain: block claudeopus.shop, bitsender.top and ecomagent.in at DNS/proxy/firewall; interview the user and revoke any Anthropic/AWS keys they may have exposed through the proxy. Treat any prompts sent as leaked. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 to find the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/AUTH_TOKEN redirect on this and other hosts; search the org for the same relay domains and for the disposable-signup domains dakaka.org, emailinbo.live, ratixq.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("claudeopus.shop","bitsender.top","ecomagent.in")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("claudeopus.shop","bitsender.top","ecomagent.in")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResolvedIP = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude Code redirected to a rogue endpoint via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN env var AIInstallation Medium
Hunts persistent user-environment registry values that repoint Claude Code (or any Anthropic SDK client) away from Anthropic to a third-party gateway. Poison Claude explicitly instructs customers to set these variables so the CLI uses its relay instead of api.anthropic.com; a BASE_URL that isn't an Anthropic host, or any value referencing the known relay domains, is the enabling config for prompt exfiltration. Rationale: Uses the exact env-var names the Poison Claude onboarding instructs customers to set (confirmed via Requesty/Anthropic env-var docs) plus a non-anthropic.com BASE_URL condition and the relay-domain IOCs. The env var persists in HKCU\Environment, giving a durable registry pivot distinct from the network UC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/poison-claude-sells-discounted-claude.html • https://www.requesty.ai/blog/claude-code-environment-variables-anthropic-base-url-auth-token • https://developer.konghq.com/cookbooks/claude-code-sso/
ATT&CKT1112 T1567
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned internal LLM gateway (LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway, Requesty, corporate proxy) legitimately setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an internal host
  • Developer pointing Claude Code at a self-hosted/on-prem Anthropic-compatible endpoint on an RFC1918 address
  • AWS Bedrock users (note: Bedrock uses CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK, not BASE_URL — should not match, but mixed configs exist)
  • QA/test automation setting the variable to a mock endpoint on localhost
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has "://localhost" or RegistryValueData has "://127.0.0.1" or RegistryValueData matches regex @"://(10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the RegistryValueData — is the endpoint an approved internal gateway, localhost/RFC1918, or an external/unknown host? Cross-check the setting user and whether the host also shows egress from UC1. 2) Contain: if the endpoint is external and unsanctioned, clear the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/AUTH_TOKEN values, block the endpoint, and rotate any Anthropic/AWS Bedrock keys the user provisioned. 3) Hunt: sweep all dev endpoints for the same env-var names pointing off-Anthropic, check ~/.claude/settings.json for an equivalent 'env' override, and correlate with UC1 relay-domain egress to scope how many prompts were routed through the proxy.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Environment"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL","ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" and RegistryValueData !has "anthropic.com" and isnotempty(RegistryValueData))
      or RegistryValueData has_any ("claudeopus.shop","bitsender.top","ecomagent.in")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "\\Environment"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL","ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
| where (RegistryValue =~ "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL" and RegistryValueData !has "anthropic.com" and isnotempty(RegistryValueData))
      or RegistryValueData has_any ("claudeopus.shop","bitsender.top","ecomagent.in")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Critical

Paperclip AI Flaws Let Attackers Run Host Commands via Malicious Agent Imports

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Two security flaws in Paperclip could let attackers execute commands on a network server or a developer's computer. Paperclip is an open-source control plane for teams of artificial intelligence (AI) agents, and both paths rely on importing a malicious agent and starting it. A third flaw could expose sensitive data and control-plane details through application programming interface (API) routes

CVEsCVE-2026-41679
ATT&CKT1190 T1539 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious .paperclip.yaml agent-import bundle written to a Paperclip host · [LLM] DNS-rebinding to loopback against local_trusted Paperclip (external hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Paperclip AI process adapter spawning an interactive shell (host command execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Paperclip AI process adapter spawning an interactive shell (host command execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the terminal impact of CVE-2026-41679 and GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7: Paperclip's built-in process adapter launching an attacker-supplied command as a child of the server process. Pivots on a Paperclip parent context spawning a shell/LOLBin, which is the article's stated 'run host commands' outcome after a malicious agent import + wakeup. Rationale: Uses the article's stated behaviour that Paperclip's 'built-in process adapter intentionally launches a configured command as a child process of the server' and pivots parent context on the product name 'paperclip' with shell/recon children — the concrete host-command-execution endpoint of both critical chains. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41679 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Paperclip agent legitimately configured with a process adapter that runs a shell wrapper or curl-based health check
  • DevOps sysadmin running Paperclip interactively from a shell whose command line still contains the 'paperclip' path
  • CI/CD job invoking the Paperclip CLI which then shells out to a build script
  • Legitimate agent that uses curl/wget to fetch data as its designed task
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("health","heartbeat","--version") and FileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm whether the shell/LOLBin maps to a sanctioned agent definition or is ad-hoc recon (whoami, id, cat /etc/passwd, curl to unknown host). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, stop the Paperclip service, and rotate the service-account credentials, board API tokens, and any secrets reachable to the agent process. 3) Hunt: check for a preceding .paperclip.yaml import and CLI-challenge self-approval, and confirm Paperclip is >= v2026.416.0; review new-company imports and open-registration accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "paperclip" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "paperclip"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh","sh","bash","zsh","dash","whoami","curl","curl.exe","wget")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "paperclip" or ParentProcessName has "paperclip"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","whoami","curl","wget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious .paperclip.yaml agent-import bundle written to a Paperclip host AIDelivery Medium
Detects creation of the .paperclip.yaml bundle used in both CVE-2026-41679 and the DNS-rebinding chain to define a new company plus a process-adapter agent and its command. This is the delivery artifact an unauthorized or browser-originated import drops before the wakeup call triggers host execution. Rationale: Keys on the exact article-named artifact '.paperclip.yaml bundle defining a new company, an agent using the process adapter, and the command that agent would run' — a concrete, high-fidelity filename that precedes host execution. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41679 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator authoring or updating a .paperclip.yaml during normal deployment/configuration
  • Version-control checkout (git) restoring a tracked .paperclip.yaml into a repo working directory
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Chef) templating out a sanctioned .paperclip.yaml
  • Developer testing a new agent locally in local_trusted mode
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","git","ansible","code.exe","Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the .paperclip.yaml and inspect for a process-adapter agent plus an embedded command; identify the writing process (browser vs Paperclip service vs editor) and the account. 2) Contain: if the bundle defines a new company with a shell/command agent from an unexpected writer, quarantine the file, stop the Paperclip service before any wakeup, and block the source. 3) Hunt: correlate to a subsequent Paperclip-parent shell spawn (UC1), review web logs for the import + wakeup sequence, and enumerate recently created companies and self-approved board CLI credentials.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ ".paperclip.yaml"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".paperclip.yaml"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS-rebinding to loopback against local_trusted Paperclip (external hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7 browser->localhost crossing: an attacker-controlled hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1 so a browser's same-origin requests reach a loopback-bound Paperclip in local_trusted mode. Surfaces DNS answers and browser connections where a public FQDN maps to the loopback interface. Rationale: Encodes the article's DNS-rebinding mechanism verbatim: an attacker hostname 'resolved to both the attacker's server and 127.0.0.1' so later requests reach the local Paperclip service — flagged as a public FQDN resolving/connecting to loopback, which is anomalous outside this attack class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8hx-rhr2-9rf7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/paperclip-ai-flaws-let-attackers-run.html
ATT&CKT1189 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Local dev tooling using a custom /etc/hosts or *.localtest.me / *.lvh.me style domain that resolves to 127.0.0.1 for HTTPS-on-localhost workflows
  • Container/dev frameworks (e.g. some Docker/mkcert setups) mapping a project FQDN to loopback
  • Split-horizon DNS or a captive-portal appliance briefly answering a public name with 127.0.0.1
  • Ad/tracker-blocking DNS (Pi-hole/hosts sinkhole) that null-routes domains to 127.0.0.1
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith "localtest.me" or RemoteUrl endswith "lvh.me" or RemoteUrl endswith ".test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving FQDN and the browser/host; determine whether the loopback answer comes from a sanctioned dev domain or a sinkhole vs an unfamiliar external domain. 2) Contain: if unexplained, capture the page/domain, block it at DNS/proxy, and confirm any loopback Paperclip is upgraded to v2026.416.0 (private-hostname guard enabled) so rebound Host headers are rejected. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for a following .paperclip.yaml import (UC2) and Paperclip-parent shell spawn (UC1), and review any local Paperclip access logs for imports/wakeup calls carrying the attacker hostname in the Host header.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1","::1")
| where RemoteUrl contains "."
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox.exe","firefox","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","Safari","Google Chrome")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where isnotempty(DstHostname)
| where DstHostname !in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1","::1")
| where DstHostname contains "."
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Rebinding to Loopback (Public Hostname Resolving to 127.0.0.1)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
