Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phishing delivery via abused trusted SaaS hosting (Workers.dev / Vercel / Railway / Firebase / Jotform) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID device code authentication flow success (EvilTokens / Kali365 / Storm-2372) · [LLM] AiTM session-cookie replay — interactive vs non-interactive geo/IP split (Tycoon 2FA / Evilginx) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra ID device code authentication flow success (EvilTokens / Kali365 / Storm-2372) AIExploitation High
Hunts successful OAuth device-code (RFC 8628) authorization grants completed by users who don't normally use that flow, and source IPs completing device-code auth for multiple accounts. Device-code phishing is the exact technique the article says has exploded from zero to 25+ criminal kits (EvilTokens, Kali365, ARToken, DEBULL, Forg365, Tycoon 2FA). Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit claim that device-code phishing kits went from zero to 25+ (EvilTokens 340+ orgs, Kali365 FBI advisory, DEBULL, Forg365, Tycoon 2FA). Detects the invariant destination behaviour the article calls out — a completed device-code auth grant — plus source-IP fan-out. Sentinel re-expressed on AuthenticationDetails per schema (AuthenticationProtocol absent from provided SigninLogs columns). Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/device-code-phishing-ai-mfa-bypass • https://spycloud.com/blog/kali365-anatomy-of-a-microsoft365-phishing-as-a-service-kit/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/debull-tooling-abuses-microsoft-device.html • https://github.com/Bert-JanP/Hunting-Queries-Detection-Rules/blob/main/Defender%20For%20Identity/SuccessfulDeviceCodeAuthentication.md
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-ins from IoT/CLI tooling (Azure CLI, PowerShell Az, smart-TV/conference-room devices) that batch multiple service accounts
  • Automated onboarding scripts registering several accounts from one admin jump host
  • Penetration test / red-team device-code exercises
  • Shared-kiosk devices where several staff complete device-code login from one egress IP
  • VDI/Citrix pools where many users share a NAT egress IP
Suppression filter
| where not (Apps has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Visual Studio Code"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged IP, confirm whether the users legitimately use device-code flow (developers/CLI vs standard office workers) and check AppDisplayName/ResourceDisplayName — Office/Graph device-code for a non-dev user is high-suspicion. 2) Contain: revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession) and reset credentials for affected users, then block device-code flow via a Conditional Access authentication-flows policy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the token from AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs to find follow-on mailbox rules, OAuth app consents, and downloads from the attacker IP/ASN.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"   // device-code grant leg
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize Users = dcount(AccountUpn), UserList = make_set(AccountUpn, 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5), Cities = make_set(City, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Users >= 2   // one source IP completing device-code auth for >=2 users/hour = campaign fan-out
| order by Users desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // AuthenticationProtocol is not in this tenant's SigninLogs schema; deviceCode protocol string surfaces inside AuthenticationDetails
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), UserList = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5), Countries = make_set(Location, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Users >= 2   // source-IP fan-out across >=2 accounts in an hour
| order by Users desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 deviceCode
CLOUD
index=azure (sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" OR sourcetype="azure:aad:signin:interactive") "status.errorCode"=0 authenticationProtocol=deviceCode
| stats dc(userPrincipalName) as user_count values(userPrincipalName) as users values(appDisplayName) as apps values(location.countryOrRegion) as countries min(_time) as firstTime by ipAddress
| where user_count>=2
| convert ctime(firstTime)
| sort - user_count
AiTM session-cookie replay — interactive vs non-interactive geo/IP split (Tycoon 2FA / Evilginx) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a successful interactive sign-in against a successful non-interactive (token-backed) sign-in for the same user from a different IP and country within one hour — the behavioural fingerprint of an AiTM proxy relaying credentials/MFA and replaying the stolen session cookie. Targets the interception invariant the article says is constant across Tycoon, Sneaky 2FA, Evilginx and 75+ forks. Rationale: Article states every AiTM kit implements the same interception invariant (proxy session, relay MFA token, capture authenticated session) and that behaviour survives infrastructure rotation. The interactive-vs-non-interactive geo/IP split within an hour is the token-replay signature. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — this join lives entirely in Entra sign-in telemetry not shipped to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/recent-oauth-attacks-detection-strategies • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/ • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/device-code-phishing
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1111
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN/roaming users whose interactive and token traffic egress from different countries
  • Mobile + laptop used simultaneously across a border region (e.g. commuter cities)
  • Cloud-hosted mail clients / Exchange Online connectors polling tokens from a datacenter IP in another country
  • Users travelling while a background service (Teams/OneDrive) still refreshes tokens from home ASN
  • Third-party SaaS integrations acting on behalf of the user from vendor IP ranges
Suppression filter
| where IntCountry != "" and NonIntCountry != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the two IPs/ASNs and UserAgents — datacenter/hosting ASN on the non-interactive leg while the interactive leg is a residential/mobile ISP strongly indicates cookie replay; check RiskLevelDuringSignIn. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens and sessions, force re-auth with phishing-resistant MFA, and quarantine any inbox rules created after the non-interactive sign-in. 3) Hunt: sweep for the attacker IP/ASN across other users, and check OAuth app grants and mailbox forwarding added in the same window.
let window = 1h;
let interactive = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where IsInteractive == true and ErrorCode == 0
    | where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
    | project IntTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, IntIP = IPAddress, IntCountry = Country, IntUA = UserAgent, Application;
interactive
| join kind=inner (
    AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where IsInteractive == false and ErrorCode == 0
    | project NonIntTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, NonIntIP = IPAddress, NonIntCountry = Country, NonIntUA = UserAgent
  ) on AccountObjectId
| where NonIntTime between (IntTime .. IntTime + window)
| where IntIP != NonIntIP and IntCountry != NonIntCountry
| project IntTime, NonIntTime, AccountUpn, IntIP, IntCountry, IntUA, NonIntIP, NonIntCountry, NonIntUA, Application
| order by IntTime desc
let window = 1h;
let interactive = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
    | project IntTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, UserPrincipalName, IntIP = IPAddress, IntCountry = Location, AppDisplayName;
interactive
| join kind=inner (
    AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | project NonIntTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, NonIntIP = IPAddress, NonIntCountry = Location
  ) on UserId
| where NonIntTime between (IntTime .. IntTime + window)
| where IntIP != NonIntIP and IntCountry != NonIntCountry
| project IntTime, NonIntTime, UserPrincipalName, IntIP, IntCountry, NonIntIP, NonIntCountry, AppDisplayName
| order by IntTime desc
CLOUD
index=azure sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "status.errorCode"=0
| eval country='location.countryOrRegion'
| stats dc(country) as country_count values(country) as countries dc(ipAddress) as ip_count values(ipAddress) as ips values(appDisplayName) as apps min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by userPrincipalName
| where country_count>1 AND ip_count>1 AND (lastTime-firstTime)<3600
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - country_count
Phishing delivery via abused trusted SaaS hosting (Workers.dev / Vercel / Railway / Firebase / Jotform) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound delivered email carrying links to the disposable trusted-hosting platforms the article names as commonly abused to inherit domain reputation, and correlates on the user actually clicking. Targets the article's point that attackers borrow reputation from platforms no blocklist would flag. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit list of abused trusted-hosting platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Railway, Google Firebase, Jotform, Google Sites) and pairs email delivery with an actual Safe Links click for fidelity. Scoped to the disposable-hosting subset (excludes sharepoint.com/dynamics.com/azure) to keep FPs manageable. Sentinel expressed on ImWebSession (proxy) since EmailEvents is not in this tenant's Sentinel schema. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/device-code-phishing • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/how-ai-powered-phishing-killed-blocklists-for-good/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate business apps hosted on Vercel/Railway/Firebase that staff routinely receive links to
  • Marketing/newsletter emails linking to Jotform surveys or Google Sites pages
  • Developers sharing preview deployments on *.vercel.app / *.pages.dev internally
  • SaaS vendor notification emails whose CDN sits on workers.dev
  • QA/staging links to firebaseapp.com project builds
Suppression filter
| where IsClickedThrough == true or DetectionMethods != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the destination page (detonate in a sandbox with a real-browser UA + referrer, since the article notes crawler-vs-victim content differs) and check the sender's authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) and whether the clicker entered credentials. 2) Contain: soft-delete the message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents/ZAP, block the specific subdomain, and if credentials were entered treat as UC-1/UC-2 (revoke sessions, reset). 3) Hunt: pivot on SenderFromAddress and the full UrlChain to find sibling disposable domains and other recipients who clicked.
let SaaS = dynamic(["workers.dev","pages.dev","vercel.app","railway.app","up.railway.app","web.app","firebaseapp.com","jotform.com","sites.google.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain has_any (SaaS)
| join kind=inner (
    UrlClickEvents

| project Timestamp, ClickTime, SenderFromAddress, Recipient = AccountUpn, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, IsClickedThrough, ClickIP
| order by ClickTime desc
let SaaS = dynamic(["workers.dev","pages.dev","vercel.app","railway.app","web.app","firebaseapp.com","jotform.com","sites.google.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstHostname has_any (SaaS) or Url has_any (SaaS)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Trojanized npm Packages Employ NullReceiver Tactic to Decode C2 IP from Blockchain

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 10 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged an evolution of the EtherHiding blockchain-based command-and-control (C2) technique that conceals the C2 server IP address inside a made-up destination address of a completely empty Ethereum transfer. The new dead drop resolver approach, observed in two trojanized npm packages "bianira-ui" and "fluid-type-ui," has been codenamed NullReceiver by

NullReceiver npm C2 beacon to hardcoded IP 166.88.134.62 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host connecting outbound to 166.88.134.62, the C2 server that the trojanized npm packages bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui decode from the recipient bytes (a6 58 86 3e) of a zero-value Ethereum transfer. Because the packages impersonate front-end Tailwind/CSS UI libraries, a node process reaching this raw IP is unambiguously malicious. Rationale: 166.88.134.62 is a hardcoded network IOC confirmed by three independent write-ups (cybersecuritynews, gbhackers, cyberpress) and the OpenSourceMalware decode flowchart, giving it near-zero false-positive risk as a direct-match alert. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korean-hackers-hiding-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/nullreceiver-wallet-trail/ • https://cyberpress.org/nullreceiver-hides-ethereum-c2/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal asset legitimately assigned 166.88.134.62 after attacker infrastructure is sinkholed/reassigned (verify current WHOIS/ASN)
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample intentionally
  • Threat-intel proxy or TAXII feed proactively probing the IOC
  • NAT egress where the IP is a shared upstream (rare for a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessCommandLine/process — expect node.exe/npm; pull the host's node_modules for bianira-ui or fluid-type-ui and the developer/user who ran the install. 2) Contain: block 166.88.134.62 at the egress firewall/EDR, isolate the host, and revoke any developer/CI credentials and npm tokens that lived on the box (DPRK Contagious Interview targets dev secrets). 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for outbound hits to this IP and for the two package names, and pivot on the attacker wallet 0xa322e5f3d311d3080e6f0121063e9adc2490ef1a to enumerate rotated C2 IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "166.88.134.62"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "166.88.134.62"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstHostname, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Install of trojanized npm packages bianira-ui / fluid-type-ui AIInstallation High
Hunts file writes into node_modules for the two known-malicious packages bianira-ui (by npmuser1101) and fluid-type-ui (by npmuser3002), which masquerade as Tailwind CSS plugins. Catches the supply-chain foothold at install time on developer workstations and CI runners regardless of the C2 IP, which rotates. Rationale: Package names bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui are corroborated by the original THN report plus cybersecuritynews and gbhackers; matching the node_modules install path yields a high-fidelity, IP-rotation-resistant detection that fires on the supply-chain foothold itself. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/north-korean-hackers-hiding-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/nullreceiver-wallet-trail/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package coincidentally named with the same string in an unrelated scoped path (unlikely given exact names)
  • Security team intentionally st[ag]ing the sample in a malware lab
  • Internal mirror/Artifactory caching the withdrawn package for IR analysis
  • Developer restoring an old lockfile that still references the removed package
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installing user and whether the package reached a runtime (node/npm parent) versus only lockfile resolution; grab package.json/package-lock.json to see how it entered the dependency tree. 2) Contain: uninstall the package, isolate the host/CI runner, rotate npm tokens, SSH keys, cloud creds and wallet keys present on the box, and purge any internal registry cache copies. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (outbound to 166.88.134.62), search all lockfiles across repos for the two names, and check for other packages from npmuser1101 and npmuser3002.

NullReceiver dead-drop: node queries Ethereum RPC then beacons to a raw IP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the NullReceiver resolution behaviour itself: a node/npm process contacts a public Ethereum RPC provider (to read the attacker wallet's last transaction) and, within 5 minutes on the same host, connects to a raw public IP with no DNS/hostname — the decoded C2. This survives C2-IP and wallet rotation and flags copycat packages the IOCs miss. Rationale: The OpenSourceMalware flowchart (null.png) confirms the sequence npm package -> public Ethereum ledger lookup -> connect to decoded raw IP; correlating a node RPC read with a same-host connection to a hostname-less public IP within 5 min captures the technique generically, catching rotated wallets/IPs that pure IOC rules miss. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/trojanized-npm-packages-decode-c2-ip.html • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhp2JlYxtO8ERLKOUQWEHhsEpf5fOczPAzfCYSUfZJCs4_O3vxIogUH1sH3pDS3TnpeQ9ctxXu0QVfTQTdt9I_BfsYl8SaF5cpY_wKimW9-tkgLOE4tYnUr7aSVDnM4d0CEMr4pYT5KiV-_mCYQMzC_vhwRQDTUunVBKiBKjgFiAPMs_A1TSBlWubYasQHK/s1700-e365/null.png
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/dapp or wallet-integration project whose node backend polls an Ethereum RPC then opens raw-IP peer connections
  • Blockchain indexer / node client (ethers.js, web3.js, hardhat) running in dev or CI
  • Crypto price-ticker or NFT tooling that reads on-chain data
  • P2P libraries (libp2p, IPFS) that dial peers by IP after a bootstrap lookup
Suppression filter
// Suppress known-good web3 projects by initiating command line / working dir
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("hardhat", "truffle", "ethers", "web3", "foundry", "ganache")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the node process's working directory and package.json — a UI/CSS-themed dependency (like Tailwind plugins) that touches Ethereum RPC is the tell; capture the raw IP it dialed. 2) Contain: block the decoded raw IP and the parent package, isolate the host, and rotate developer/CI secrets. 3) Hunt: enrich the raw IP against threat intel, pivot the host's process tree for the trojanized package names, and add the newly-observed C2 IP and any new attacker wallet addresses to the IOC watchlist for org-wide sweeping.
let LookbackDays = 30d;

let RpcHosts = dynamic(["mainnet.infura.io","eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com","cloudflare-eth.com","rpc.ankr.com","ethereum.publicnode.com","api.etherscan.io","etherscan.io","eth.llamarpc.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","rpc.flashbots.net"]);
let BlockchainLookups = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm")
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (RpcHosts)
    | project RpcTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RpcHost = RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl)
| join kind=inner BlockchainLookups on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (RpcTime .. RpcTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| project RpcTime, RawIpTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, RpcHost, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by RawIpTime desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New OVSwrap Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Open vSwitch

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A memory corruption flaw in the Linux kernel's Open vSwitch datapath gives ordinary local users a path to root on a broad set of default-configured distributions, and a public exploit ships with pre-built records for roughly 800 kernel builds. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-64531 (CVSS score: 7.8) and codenamed OVSwrap by its discoverer, was disclosed by security researcher Asim

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OVSwrap privesc: unprivileged `unshare -Urn` to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN in new netns · [LLM] OVSwrap: openvswitch kernel module load/autoload on a host that doesn't run ovs-vswitchd · [LLM] OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New OVSwrap Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Open vSwitch
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
OVSwrap privesc: unprivileged `unshare -Urn` to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN in new netns AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap (CVE-2026-64531) entry step where an ordinary local user runs `unshare -Urn` to create private user+network namespaces and gain CAP_NET_ADMIN inside them, the prerequisite for reaching the vulnerable Open vSwitch flow-installation path. This is the exact invocation the public PoC uses to start the chain on default-configured distros. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC command `unshare -Urn` (creating user+network namespaces to gain CAP_NET_ADMIN); non-root actor excludes normal privileged container tooling. Corroborated against CloudLinux and securityonline write-ups of the same PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/ • https://securityonline.info/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-local-root/ • https://cloudlinux.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/29223197225116-Kernel-Local-Privilege-Escalation-CVE-2026-64531-OVSwrap-Open-vSwitch-Affected-Status-and-Fix
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container runtimes (Podman/rootless Docker, LXC, bubblewrap) legitimately creating user+net namespaces
  • CI/CD sandboxing jobs using unshare for isolation
  • Developers testing network namespaces manually
  • Flatpak/snap application launches that spin up namespaces
  • nsenter/unshare used by systemd or debugging tooling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("podman","dockerd","containerd","runc","lxc-start","bwrap","flatpak","snap","systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the unshare PID on the host — is the parent an interactive shell of a non-service user, and does an openvswitch module load or sudoers write follow within seconds? 2) Contain: if the actor is untrusted/multi-tenant, freeze the account, snapshot the host, and apply the module block `echo 'install openvswitch /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/ovswrap.conf` then unload/reboot. 3) Hunt: search the same host and user for subsequent `modprobe/insmod openvswitch`, `aa-exec -p trinity`, and writes to /etc/sudoers* — confirming the OVSwrap chain vs. benign namespace usage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "unshare"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-Urn","-rUn","-Unr") or (ProcessCommandLine has "--user" and ProcessCommandLine has "--net" and (ProcessCommandLine has "--map-root-user" or ProcessCommandLine has "-r"))
| where AccountName != "root" and AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/unshare" or TargetProcessName == "unshare"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-Urn","-rUn") or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--user" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--net")
| where ActorUsername != "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OVSwrap CVE-2026-64531 Unprivileged unshare User+Net Namespace Creation

OVSwrap: openvswitch kernel module load/autoload on a host that doesn't run ovs-vswitchd AIExploitation Medium
Hunts loading of the vulnerable openvswitch datapath module via modprobe/insmod — the OVSwrap exploit triggers auto-load by resolving the Generic Netlink family name, so the module can appear even where lsmod was previously empty and ovs-vswitchd is not deployed. On non-OVS/OpenStack hosts this load is anomalous and a direct signal of CVE-2026-64531 exploitation prep. Rationale: Uses the article's specific module name `openvswitch` and the auto-load-by-genl-family behaviour it calls out; scoping to hosts that don't run ovs-vswitchd makes the module load high-signal. Confirmed as the exploited component in SentinelOne and CloudLinux advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-64531/ • https://cloudlinux.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/29223197225116-Kernel-Local-Privilege-Escalation-CVE-2026-64531-OVSwrap-Open-vSwitch-Affected-Status-and-Fix
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OpenStack / OVN / OVS hypervisor and network nodes loading openvswitch at boot
  • systemd-modules-load.service or /etc/modules-load.d loading OVS on networking hosts
  • Kubernetes CNI plugins (e.g. OVN-Kubernetes, Antrea) loading the datapath
  • Admin manually enabling Open vSwitch for a new bridge
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Puppet) provisioning OVS on network infra
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["ovs-node-01","ovs-node-02"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd","systemd-modules-load","ansible","puppet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a legitimate OVS/OpenStack/OVN/CNI node (is ovs-vswitchd installed and enabled?). If not, treat the load as suspicious. 2) Contain: on non-OVS hosts, deploy `echo 'install openvswitch /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/ovswrap.conf`, then unload the resident module (`modprobe -r openvswitch`) or schedule a reboot; isolate if multi-tenant. 3) Hunt: correlate a preceding `unshare -Urn` by a non-root user and any following /etc/sudoers* writes or new root shells on the same host to confirm the OVSwrap chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "openvswitch"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Loads=count(),
            SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
            by DeviceName, AccountName, FileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/modprobe","/insmod","/kmod") or TargetProcessName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "openvswitch"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) AIExploitation High
Detects the OVSwrap PoC's AppArmor bypass fallback — where direct namespace creation is blocked on Ubuntu 24.04, the exploit re-runs itself under the permissive `trinity` profile via `aa-exec -p trinity` to restore reachability to the vulnerable path. The `aa-exec -p trinity` string is a near-unique PoC artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC artifact `aa-exec -p trinity`, an AppArmor-confinement bypass specific to the OVSwrap exploit on Ubuntu 24.04 — extremely unlikely to appear in benign administration. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://pbxscience.com/ovswrap-flaw-in-linux-kernels-open-vswitch-lets-local-users-become-root/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A site that legitimately ships a custom AppArmor profile literally named 'trinity'
  • Security researchers reproducing the OVSwrap PoC in an authorized lab
  • AppArmor profile testing/QA that invokes aa-exec with a named profile
  • Automated exploit-detection or vuln-scanning tooling replaying the PoC
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is near-unique to the PoC — immediately confirm the host, actor, and whether a 'trinity' AppArmor profile even legitimately exists there (`aa-status`). 2) Contain: isolate the host, freeze the invoking account, capture memory/process tree; on Ubuntu re-enable the userns AppArmor restriction and apply the openvswitch module block. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the full chain — preceding `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, and following /etc/sudoers* modification or unexpected uid=0 shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "aa-exec"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "trinity"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/aa-exec" or TargetProcessName == "aa-exec"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "trinity" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap PoC's post-root action — after corrupting a kernel credential it modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to entrench root access before opening a root shell. Flags writes to these paths by processes that are not the sanctioned sudoers editors or package/config-management tooling. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit post-exploit action — the PoC modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to persist root — and filters the known-good editors/package managers so only anomalous writers surface. Datadog left empty: the linux.auditd standard schema exposes process/user fields but not a reliable file-path attribute for this write. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef/Salt) deploying sudoers drop-ins
  • cloud-init seeding sudoers for a new cloud instance's default user
  • Admin adding a sudo rule via a text editor instead of visudo
  • Package post-install scripts dropping files into /etc/sudoers.d
  • IdM/SSSD or FreeIPA tooling syncing sudo rules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","ansible","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written sudoers content and identify the writing process and user — a non-editor writer (e.g. an exploit binary or unexpected shell) adding NOPASSWD/ALL for a normal user is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: revert the sudoers change, revoke/reset the affected account, isolate the host and preserve the file plus process tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for the OVSwrap precursors — `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, `aa-exec -p trinity` — and any root shell spawned immediately after the write; patch to a fixed vendor kernel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath == "/etc/sudoers" or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init","unattended-upgr")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath == "/etc/sudoers" or TargetFilePath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate","FileWrite")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN

Kali365 Weaponizes Microsoft Authentication Against US Companies: New Enterprise Risk

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Kali365 is turning a legitimate Microsoft login into a gateway to corporate data. The phishing kit targets US organizations with attacker-controlled device codes that victims approve on Microsoft's real authentication page. Once access and refresh tokens are issued, attackers may retain access to email, documents, and cloud resources, creating a direct path to data exposure, financial fraud,

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth device-code grant, which Kali365 abuses to have victims approve an attacker-generated code on Microsoft's real login page. Device-code flow is legitimate but rare for interactive knowledge workers, making its appearance on a normal user account a high-value pivot for token theft. Rationale: Uses the article's core TTP — attacker-controlled device codes approved on Microsoft's legitimate device-login portal — expressed as the OAuth device-code grant, which is the single defining signal of Kali365 token issuance. AuthenticationProtocol not being an available column in this tenant's SigninLogs schema, the flow is matched on the deviceCode marker inside AuthenticationDetails. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers authenticating Azure CLI / Azure PowerShell on a shell that cannot pop a browser
  • Conference-room / Teams Rooms and smart-TV devices enrolling via device code
  • IoT or headless kiosk provisioning that legitimately uses the device-code grant
  • Developers logging into az login --use-device-code over SSH
  • New MDM/Intune device onboarding using device-code sign-in
Suppression filter
| where not (Application has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and DeviceTrustType == "Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the user's device-code sign-ins — check the resource/app requested, source IP geo, and whether the user owns a headless/CLI workflow that would explain it. Compare the sign-in IP to the user's normal locations. 2. Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-MFA; block the source IP. 3. Hunt: enumerate all OAuth tokens/apps consented for the account, review mailbox rules and recent mail/file access, and search other users for device-code sign-ins from the same IP/ASN within 24h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in the auth-detail JSON
| where ErrorCode == 0                            // completed sign-in => token issued
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20),
            Apps = make_set(Application, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in AuthenticationDetails JSON
| where ResultType == 0                           // successful sign-in
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc

CLOUD

| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("properties.ipAddress") as ipAddress values("properties.appDisplayName") as app values("properties.resourceDisplayName") as resource dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount by user
